Cette dynamique implique une réduction de la charge idéologique présente dans son œuvre antérieure et réaffirme, presque comme une thèse narrative, la prémisse selon laquelle l’argent peut tout. La conséquence directe de cette posture est une fin heureuse, dépourvue des aspérités conflictuelles qui caractérisaient sa production précédente.

À l’opposé du spectre littéraire, Gustavo Martín Garzo réaffirme son intérêt permanent pour les mythes de diverses traditions, les adaptant à sa tâche créative jusqu’à les intégrer comme partie intrinsèque de sa voix. L’auteur avait déjà réalisé cet exercice auparavant avec la légende du Minotaure dans *Le Jardin doré*, avec l’héritage des contes d’Andersen et des frères Grimm dans *Trois contes de fées*, ou avec les Évangiles bibliques dans *Le Langage des sources*. Avec *Un paradis de ruines*, Garzo porte cette pratique à un niveau d’explicitation supérieur. Il s’agit d’un volume réunissant quatorze récits dédiés à explorer différentes figures de la mythologie hellénique. L’éventail thématique est large : il va d’Atalante, déesse associée aux courses et à la précision à la chasse, jusqu’à Pasiphaé, l’épouse de Minos qui, après s’être unie à un taureau, donna naissance au monstre habitant le labyrinthe crétois.

La proposition de Martín Garzo consiste à réexaminer ces récits mythologiques et à leur conférer une texture romanesque facilitant leur approche par le lecteur moderne. Pour ce faire, il modifie la perspective narrative : parfois, c’est un personnage secondaire du mythe qui prend la parole, comme c’est le cas avec l’architecte Dédale. Dans d’autres cas, il laisse parler directement le personnage mythique lui-même, tel est le cas de Nausicaa, fille d’Alcinoos, roi des Phéaciens. Dans la narration traditionnelle, Nausicaa rencontra Ulysse sur une plage et le présenta à son père, qui lui fournit le navire nécessaire pour regagner Ithaque. Cependant, la vision de Garzo nuance ces personnages classiques. L’écrivain présente un héros de *L’Odyssée* qui passe ses journées à dormir et qui pourrait être un menteur compulsif, en contraste avec une Nausicaa qui tombe éperdument amoureuse de ses os et de ses aventures, qu’elles soient réelles ou fictives. À travers ces réinterprétations, l’amour se consolide comme le véritable protagoniste de cet excellent livre, devenant par ailleurs la grande découverte littéraire qui confère une cohésion inhabituelle à tous les mythes classiques que le lecteur connaît.

La célèbre réflexion de Karl Marx dans *Le 18 Brumaire de Louis Bonaparte*, selon laquelle les grands événements historiques se produisent deux fois — la première comme tragédie, la seconde comme farce —, résonne avec une actualité inquiétante. Bien que le philosophe allemand parodie Hegel, dont la figure reste généralement dans l’oubli populaire, la prémisse s’avère inévitablement applicable à l’analyse contemporaine. Andrés Ollero aborde cette dynamique dans son œuvre *Et il semble que ce fut hier…*, où il dissèque la fin de cycle des gouvernements de Felipe González sous le sous-titre révélateur de *La législature de l’épuisement du changement*. La lecture de ces pages s’avère idéale pour comprendre la conjoncture actuelle, établissant un miroir critique avec le présent.

L’ouvrage se présente comme une compilation rigoureuse qui entrelace des textes publiés à l’origine par l’auteur avec de nouvelles articulations conférant continuité et profondeur historique à l’examen de la décennie 1990. À travers ses chapitres, Ollero dresse le portrait d’une galerie d’épisodes déterminants : les scandales de corruption, l’« affaire Roldán », les stratégies déployées pour contrôler l’information, les actions discutables de l’État et de ses structures opaques, les échecs structurels dans le domaine de l’éducation et, bien sûr, l’usure inévitable résultant de tant d’années ininterrompues au pouvoir.

Bien qu’Ollero n’épargne pas la critique ni n’évite de mentionner sa propre participation à ces événements – en raison de son affiliation au Parti populaire et des fonctions qu’il a occupées durant ces années –, le portrait politique qui en émerge reste nuancé. Il convient toutefois de souligner la présence d’un groupe de socialistes qui conservent une image positive et sont demeurés des figures importantes, ce qui contraste avec l’évaluation d’autres personnalités. Cette dualité invite le lecteur à un exercice de réflexion comparative, l’incitant à rechercher avec attention les parallèles entre ce moment d’épuisement et la réalité politique actuelle.
title_en: Antonia Lassa ties the killers to her signature
body_en:
Police fiction has made the practice of a criminal leaving a distinctive mark on their victims or at the crime scene an almost obligatory trope. This narrative device, common in the noir genre, serves precise technical functions: on one hand, it unsettles the reader by dehumanizing the murderer, endowing them with monstrous psychology; on the other, it initially aids the protagonist tasked with their capture, as that signature acts as a warning that the crimes stem from a single perpetrator with an identifiable *modus operandi*. However, this apparent help often serves a playful and strategic purpose within the plot: the psychopath toys with the hero, throwing down a challenge that turns what seemed a clear clue into a factor of misdirection and despair.

Fiction abounds with paradigmatic examples. In *The Snowman*, Norwegian writer Jo Nesbø presents a criminal who carries out his atrocities after the first winter snowfall, leaving as his signature the figure that gives the work its title. In reality, the so-called "Monster of Florence," active between 1968 and 1985, left a macabre trail by slashing the genitalia of couples he surprised at night in isolated areas.

It is within this tradition that *One Finger Less*, the second noir novel by Basque author Luisa Etxenike (San Sebastián, 1957), is set. Published under the heteronym—preferred by the writer herself over "pseudonym"—Antonia Lassa, the murderer’s signature in this case is the absence of the index finger on bodies found lifeless and disfigured in San Sebastián’s Polloe cemetery.

The investigation falls to Emilia Castro Urrutia, a deputy commissioner with the Ertzaintza. The author has imbued this character with a rare sensitivity that sits comfortably alongside her rationality, practicality, and sharp intuition for solving crime. Yet Emilia is no one-dimensional figure; she carries her own burdens, not least a failed relationship. Her daily life unfolds alongside her grandfather, an elderly former fisherman—a quintessential Basque *arrantzale*—who struggles to accept his new life as a widower. This family dynamic infuses the story with warmth and a gentle humor, humanizing the narrative through sharp, engaging dialogue. A fine example appears on page 12, where the grandfather recalls: “I told Itziar time and again, ‘Don’t you dare die before me—I couldn’t live without you.’ And she never listened.”

The plot of *Un dedo menos* grows more intricate for its protagonist, Antonia Lassa, when her initial inquiry expands beyond the local. The case begins with the discovery of a homeless man’s body inside a mausoleum in the cemetery where he was found. But the Ertzaintza deputy commissioner soon finds herself confronting a far broader pattern—one that stretches beyond the Basque Country to cities across Spain. The emergence of other bodies in Gijón, Segovia, and Madrid, all bearing the same distinctive amputation, forces Lassa to collaborate with officers from the Spanish National Police.

This novel defies the conventions of traditional *noir*. Its author, Luisa Etxenike, brings to this foray into crime fiction a rich literary background, with more than a dozen novels and two collections of short stories to her name. That experience shapes the book’s construction, which transcends the usual criminological focus or the intricate plotting of a *thriller* with its reliance on suspense and mystery. Instead, the work ventures into moral reflection, probing psychological depths and philosophical questions. It interrogates the roots of evil, dissects guilt and innocence, and examines the fragile line that separates them.

In another editorial sphere, and just weeks after the tragic death of Iranian-born author Marjane Satrapi (born in Rasht, Iran, in 1969 and deceased in 2026), a meticulously curated edition of her masterpiece *Persepolis* has reached the market. First published in France in 2000, the graphic novel is being revived by Reservoir Books to mark the 25th anniversary of its original French release. The commemorative edition restores the original format in a slipcase containing four volumes distinguished by color. It also includes a special prologue dedicated to the anniversary of this exceptional work—a comic imbued with sharp irony that, with a touch of humor, reflects the principles of its creator, a staunch advocate for justice and equality.

*Persepolis* weaves together the story of a nation and the coming-of-age journey of a young girl who struggles to comprehend the chaos around her. Refusing to accept intolerance or be dictated to about what music she should listen to, she embodies the defiance of a child caught in forces beyond her control. The work depicts the Iranian Islamic Revolution through the eyes of a ten-year-old desperate to escape a reality that overwhelms her. As the narrative unfolds, the protagonist must navigate the imposition of the veil while witnessing the seismic shifts transforming her country.

Antonia Lassa has drawn a direct connection between the assassins' signature and the author herself, in a context overshadowed by the recent and devastating loss of Marjane Satrapi. The book’s presentation had been scheduled before the heartbreaking news of her death broke. Her family attributed her passing at just 56 to profound grief, a loss that has dealt a heavy blow to the world of comics and the visual arts.

Satrapi’s graphic novel, later adapted into a critically acclaimed animated film that invites deep reflection, offers a searing critique of Muslim society through the eyes of its cartoonist and screenwriter. The author, whose other celebrated works include *Embroideries*, *Chicken with Plums*, *Woman, Life, Freedom*, and *Ajdar*, spent her formative years under the ayatollahs’ regime before emigrating to France. There, she connected with the L’Association collective of cartoonists, finding immediate kinship with the group.

Buoyed by this circle of friends, Satrapi translated her memories and experiences into comic panels, shaping her most acclaimed work, which was initially published as a series. Its first installment won the *Coup de coeur* award for best emerging author at the prestigious Angoulême International Comics Festival—a recognition that opened the door to a long list of accolades, including the Ignatz Award for Best Graphic Novel and, more recently, the Princess of Asturias Award for Communication and Humanities in 2024. The film adaptation of *Persepolis*, released in 2007, received the Jury Prize at the 60th Cannes Film Festival.

In a different narrative vein, Kathryn Stockett—born in Jackson, Mississippi, in 1969 and author of the novel *The Help* (originally published in 2009 and adapted for film in 2016)—now presents *The Unbreakables Club*. This new work echoes yet diverges from her first book. Set in 1930s Mississippi, the story required meticulous research to recreate the city of Oxford, not far from Jackson, including its landscapes and customs.

The writer sustains the reader’s attention through a plot in which two women and a girl pursue their dreams: Birdie seeks to escape poverty and pay off her debts, while Meg fights to reunite with her mother. These are the central threads of the narrative, with Meg and Birdie’s mother, Charlie, also searching for Meg’s return.

Contemporary literature’s latest publications offer two distinct narrative trajectories that, though disparate in tone and structure, share a common interest in reinterpreting the established. On one hand, Kathryn Stockett’s work marks a notable evolution from her earlier writing, while on the other, Gustavo Martín Garzo deepens his engagement with classical mythology.

In Stockett’s novel, the detailed descriptions of the protagonists’ clothing and cuisine serve as one of the most solid stylistic pillars of her writing. However, the architecture of the plot rests on the foundations of melodrama and the conventions of the serial novel, genres that allow for the inclusion of unexpected incidents to sustain narrative tension. Compared to her previous bestseller, *The Help*, this new work presents an author who is less biting in her social critique. The key to this shift lies in the mechanism through which the protagonists achieve their goals: prostitution, understood here as a self-managed activity, and the economic power it generates. This dynamic entails a reduction in the ideological weight of her earlier work and reinforces, almost as a narrative thesis, the premise that money can buy anything. The direct consequence of this stance is a happy ending, devoid of the conflicting edges that characterized her previous output.

At the opposite end of the literary spectrum, Gustavo Martín Garzo reaffirms his enduring interest in myths from various traditions, adapting them to his creative work until they become an intrinsic part of his voice. The author had previously undertaken this exercise with the legend of the Minotaur in *The Golden Garden*, with the legacy of Andersen’s and the Brothers Grimm’s fairy tales in *Three Fairy Tales*, and with the biblical Gospels in *The Language of the Springs*. Now, with *A Paradise of Rubble*, Garzo takes this practice to a higher level of explicitness. This volume brings together fourteen narrative pieces dedicated to exploring different figures from Greek mythology. The thematic range is broad: it spans from Atalanta, the goddess associated with racing and hunting accuracy, to Pasiphaë, the wife of Minos who, after mating with a bull, gave birth to the monster that inhabited the Cretan labyrinth.

Martín Garzo’s proposal involves revisiting these mythological stories and giving them a novelistic texture that makes them more accessible to the modern reader. To achieve this, he alters the narrative perspective: at times, it is a secondary character from the myth who takes the floor, as is the case with the architect Daedalus. In other instances, he allows the mythological figure themselves to speak directly, such as Nausicaa, daughter of Alcinous, king of the Phaeacians. In traditional narrative, Nausicaa encounters Odysseus on a beach and introduces him to her father, who provides the ship necessary for his return to Ithaca. However, Garzo’s vision nuances these classic characters. The writer presents an *Odyssey* hero who spends his days sleeping and may be a compulsive liar, in contrast to a Nausicaa who falls deeply in love with his adventures—real or imagined. Through these reinterpretations, love emerges as the true protagonist of this excellent book, becoming the great literary discovery that lends unusual cohesion to all the classical myths the reader knows.

Karl Marx’s famous reflection in *The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte*—which holds that great historical events occur twice, the first time as tragedy and the second as farce—resonates with unsettling relevance. Though the German philosopher was parodying Hegel, whose figure often fades into popular oblivion, the premise proves inevitably applicable to contemporary analysis. Andrés Ollero explores this dynamic in his work *And It Seems Like Yesterday…*, where he dissects the end of the cycle of Felipe González’s governments under the revealing subtitle *The Legislature of the Exhaustion of Change*. Reading these pages offers an impeccable understanding of the current situation, holding up a critical mirror to the present.

The book is structured as a rigorous compilation that weaves together texts originally published by the author with new material that provides continuity and historical depth to the examination of the 1990s. Through its chapters, Ollero explores a gallery of defining episodes: corruption scandals, the “Roldán case,” the strategies deployed to control information, questionable actions by the State and its opaque structures, structural failures in the education system, and, of course, the inevitable wear and tear resulting from so many uninterrupted years in power.

While Ollero does not shy away from criticism or avoid mentioning his own involvement in those events—given his affiliation with the People’s Party (Partido Popular) and the positions he held during those years—the political portrait that emerges is nuanced. Yet the presence of a group of Socialists who maintained a positive image and remained relevant figures stands out, contrasting with the assessment of other characters. This duality invites readers to engage in a comparative exercise of reflection, carefully seeking parallels between that moment of exhaustion and today’s political reality.

title: Racing de Santander y Alavés en directo
body:
La última jornada de trabajo antes del inicio oficial del campeonato exige precisión y atención al detalle. El Deportivo Alavés utiliza este encuentro como la ocasión definitiva para afinar el juego colectivo y corregir las pequeñas imperfecciones que puedan haber persistido durante las semanas previas. El rival elegido para este último ensayo de alto nivel es el Racing de Santander, un equipo que llega a este partido con el estatus de recién ascendido a la máxima categoría del fútbol español.

Este duelo tiene lugar en el marco de la tercera edición del Trofeo Nando Yosu, un torneo amistoso que sirve de colofón a la preparación pretemporal del club vitoriano. Bajo la dirección técnica de Quique Sánchez Flores, los babazorros buscan cerrar la fase de preparación con una victoria que sirva de impulso moral y táctico de cara a los compromisos competitivos. La afición y los seguidores del equipo tienen la oportunidad de seguir en directo cada minuto de este partido, que actúa como la prueba de fuego final antes de afrontar la primera jornada de la temporada regular.

El resultado de este enfrentamiento contra los racinguistas será, en gran medida, indicativo del estado de forma y cohesión del grupo que Sánchez Flores ha ido construyendo. Tras este compromiso amistoso, el calendario del Alavés se vuelve competitivo y exigente: el próximo sábado 15 de agosto, a las 19:30 horas, el equipo vitoriano disputará su primer partido oficial de la temporada en el estadio de Mendizorroza, donde recibirá al Getafe CF. Este encuentro marcará el verdadero comienzo de la campaña liguera, por lo que la importancia de este último entrenamiento oficial ante el Racing de Santander no puede ser subestimada.

En un contexto distinto, pero también vinculado a la protección del consumidor, se recuerda la importancia de la cautela ante las urgencias domésticas. La Organización de Consumidores y Usuarios (OCU) advierte sobre los riesgos de acudir a servicios de reparación sin la debida diligencia, especialmente cuando la necesidad es inmediata. Antes de firmar cualquier factura o dar por cerrado un servicio técnico, es fundamental seguir las recomendaciones establecidas para evitar posibles estafas o cobros injustificados. La prisa no debe ser excusa para dejar de verificar la transparencia del precio y la calidad del servicio prometido, garantizando así que los derechos del consumidor no sean vulnerados en momentos de vulnerabilidad.

original_body:
